intro: A single design can move from a printed sheet to a polished panel, plaster wall or cast vessel. Look for the process in the edges, reflections and relief.
alt: Vietnamese woodblock color, glossy dark Vietnamese lacquer, a weathered Dunhuang-style painting and a dark carved-looking bronze vessel.

variants.name: Đông Hồ print
variants.look: Bold leaf-green and red shapes sit on bright pearly paper.
variants.history: Đông Hồ’s Vietnamese folk prints are made from carved wooden blocks and traditionally use colors and papers prepared with natural materials, including shell powder in the paper coat.
variants.when: Create a festive print designed for circulation.
variants.why: A strong outline and a separate color for each printing block keep the design legible.

source.label: UNESCO | Đông Hồ folk woodblock printing

variants.name: Vietnamese lacquer painting
variants.look: Glossy red and black layers show flecks of gold and white eggshell.
variants.history: Twentieth-century Vietnamese artists developed lacquer painting into a modern fine-art medium, building on local lacquer craft. Layers are sanded and polished to bring out their colors and inserts.
variants.when: Show fine fragments inside a dark reflective surface.
variants.why: The polishing process can expose multiple depths and let eggshell add variations within a light shape.

source.label: Vietnam National Fine Arts Museum | Lacquer painting

variants.name: Dunhuang Buddhist murals
variants.look: Ribbon-like figures curl around the portrait on worn turquoise and ochre plaster.
variants.history: The Mogao caves at Dunhuang contain Buddhist murals and sculptures produced over many centuries along routes connecting China and Central Asia.
variants.when: Study how a repeated painted form can bring motion to a wall or vault.
variants.why: Long curves and rhythmic color changes lead the eye through an expansive surface.

variants.name: Chinese ritual bronze
variants.look: A symmetrical relief pattern repeats around the dark bronze vessel.
variants.history: Early Chinese bronze vessels were made for ritual offerings and other uses. During the Shang and Zhou periods, many vessels bore complex repeating relief patterns.
variants.when: Shape a vessel whose design can be read from several sides.
variants.why: Shallow relief uses the changing angle of light to emphasize the contours and ornament.

source.label: The Met | Chinese ritual bronze in the collection

prompt: Make one square image with four independently composed equal-size square artworks in an exact 2x2 grid, precise split on each midpoint, full bleed with no gutters. Four kinds of real-looking art objects, each adapting the same fictional character, with fully recognizable glasses and neat low bun.. The attached portrait is just a character reference. Our character is a 30-year-old woman with light ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, black rectangular glasses always visible, tailored charcoal knee-length sheath dress and fitted blazer with an azure pocket square, blue lanyard, little four-color windowpane clip when feasible. She holds a signature white coffee mug. Freeze identity, repeat the subject in every distinct art idiom. Copy no reference card composition or type. No writing, digits, words or labels; no diptych or pastiche. top left: Vietnamese Đông Hồ woodblock print under red and leaf-green ink fields on warm pearlescent paper, flat bold curved strokes. top right: Vietnamese lacquer painting, shiny dark red and black with a few gold leaf accents and pearl-white eggshell crackle in shirt highlights. bottom left: Dunhuang cave mural inspired, opaque mineral turquoise, faded orange and indigo on worn plaster, billowing ribbons around portrait and detailed border. bottom right: Shang-inspired bronze ritual vessel, near-black olive patina with ornate low relief, broad symmetrical prominent square eyeglasses and low bun as simplified repeating heraldic figure on the central panel above geometric spirals.
